name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey places religious organizations within the broader Other Services category (NAICS 81), where 11.3 percent of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, down slightly from 11.6 percent in the prior period. That figure is the only official government measure available and covers a wide mix of organizations beyond congregations alone, so it should be read as a rough ceiling rather than a precise count of AI-using churches.

On the question of what AI is actually doing inside congregations, the clearest picture comes from Barna Group, whose national research tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US ministry leaders. Barna's findings point to sermon preparation as a prominent and contested use case: nearly all pastors worry AI could misread scripture, and most want AI to present every interpretation of a difficult passage rather than settle on a single answer. That preference signals how clergy are thinking about the tool, useful for surfacing options but not trusted to reach conclusions on matters of doctrine or proclamation. Notre Dame's Meghan Sullivan goes further, arguing that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily.

The platform most directly building for this market is Gloo, which describes itself as a values-aligned AI provider used by faith-based organizations across the United States. Gloo's offering includes specialized language models, a developer studio with API support for inference and retrieval-augmented generation workflows, knowledge graph infrastructure for unifying congregational data, and purpose-built agents designed to coordinate ministry workflows. The company frames its work around an evaluation framework it describes as the first of its kind, measuring AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing, which reflects the sector's distinctive requirement that technology conform to theological and ethical commitments rather than the reverse.

The ethics infrastructure around this sector is unusually developed relative to its size. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, convenes technologists, theologians, and ethicists with the explicit goal of injecting what it calls humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected both, drawing on literary, classical, and oral traditions alongside religious ones. Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good separately funds interdisciplinary research on AI's impact on faith and religious life, and Pope Leo XIV has signaled that AI will be a sustained focus of his papacy, explicitly connecting the moment to Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical on the Industrial Revolution. That papal framing, noted by Notre Dame's Sullivan, suggests that for Catholic institutions in particular, formal doctrinal guidance on AI deployment may be forthcoming and will carry institutional weight.

For a decision-maker considering AI deployment in a congregational setting, the honest picture from these sources is that the sector is experimenting cautiously and that the most active vendors are building specifically for faith contexts rather than adapting generic enterprise tools. Administrative tasks and data unification appear to carry less theological friction than anything touching worship, preaching, or pastoral care, where the sources suggest strong and principled resistance. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research and Pew Research Center both track congregational technology trends and clergy attitudes respectively, and their ongoing survey work would be the appropriate places to monitor how quickly that resistance shifts or hardens as tools improve.
